[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Italy_national_football_team_Euro_2012_final.jpg/250px-Italy_national_football_team_Euro_2012_final.jpg)](/wiki/File:Italy_national_football_team_Euro_2012_final.jpg)

[The *Azzurri*](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team") in 2012. [Football](/wiki/Football_in_Italy "Football in Italy") is the most popular sport in Italy.

The most popular sport is [football](/wiki/Football_in_Italy "Football in Italy").[[420]](#cite_note-426) Italy's [team](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team") is one of the most successful, with four [World Cup](/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup") victories ([1934](/wiki/1934_FIFA_World_Cup "1934 FIFA World Cup"), [1938](/wiki/1938_FIFA_World_Cup "1938 FIFA World Cup"), [1982](/wiki/1982_FIFA_World_Cup "1982 FIFA World Cup"), and [2006](/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup")) and two [UEFA Euro](/wiki/UEFA_Euro "UEFA Euro") victories ([1968](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1968 "UEFA Euro 1968") and [2020](/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2020 "UEFA Euro 2020")).[[421]](#cite_note-427) Italian clubs have won 48 major European trophies, making Italy the second most successful country in Europe, after Spain. Italy's top league is [Serie A](/wiki/Serie_A "Serie A") and is followed by millions of fans around the world.[[422]](#cite_note-428)

Other popular team sports include basketball, volleyball, and rugby.[[423]](#cite_note-sportface-429) Italy's male and female national volleyball teams are often featured among the world's best. The [men's team](/wiki/Italy_men%27s_national_volleyball_team "Italy men's national volleyball team") won three consecutive [World Championships](/wiki/FIVB_Volleyball_Men%27s_World_Championship "FIVB Volleyball Men's World Championship") (in 1990, 1994, and 1998). Sahara :: Climate :: Precipitation :: chunk_0005
The average annual rainfall ranges from very low in the northern and southern fringes of the desert to nearly non-existent over the central and the eastern part. The thin northern fringe of the desert receives more winter cloudiness and rainfall due to the arrival of [low pressure systems](/wiki/Low_pressure_system "Low pressure system") over the Mediterranean Sea along the polar front, although very attenuated by the rain shadow effects of the mountains and the annual average rainfall ranges from 100 millimetres (4 in) to 250 millimetres (10 in). For example, [Biskra](/wiki/Biskra "Biskra"), Algeria, and [Ouarzazate](/wiki/Ouarzazate "Ouarzazate"), Morocco, are found in this zone. The southern fringe of the desert along the border with the Sahel receives summer cloudiness and rainfall due to the arrival of the Intertropical Convergence Zone from the south and the annual average rainfall ranges from 100 millimetres (4 in) to 250 millimetres (10 in). For example, Timbuktu, Mali and [Agadez](/wiki/Agadez "Agadez"), Niger are found in this zone.

The vast central hyper-arid core of the desert is virtually never affected by northerly or southerly atmospheric disturbances and permanently remains under the influence of the strongest anticyclonic weather regime, and the annual average rainfall can drop to less than 1 millimetre (0.04 in). In fact, most of the Sahara receives less than 20 millimetres (0.8 in). Of the 9,000,000 square kilometres (3,500,000 sq mi) of desert land in the Sahara, an area of about 2,800,000 square kilometres (1,100,000 sq mi) (about 31% of the total area) receives an annual average rainfall amount of 10 millimetres (0.4 in) or less, while some 1,500,000 square kilometres (580,000 sq mi) (about 17% of the total area) receives an average of 5 millimetres (0.2 in) or less.[[25]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-25)

The regular icosahedron inside the regular dodecahedron

The [dual polyhedron](/wiki/Dual_polyhedron "Dual polyhedron") of a dodecahedron is the [regular icosahedron](/wiki/Regular_icosahedron "Regular icosahedron"). One property of the dual polyhedron generally is that the original polyhedron and its dual share the same [three-dimensional symmetry group](/wiki/Point_groups_in_three_dimensions "Point groups in three dimensions"). In the case of the regular dodecahedron, it has the same symmetry as the regular icosahedron, the [icosahedral symmetry](/wiki/Icosahedral_symmetry "Icosahedral symmetry")

When a regular dodecahedron is inscribed in a [sphere](/wiki/Sphere "Sphere"), it occupies more of the sphere's volume (66.49%) than an icosahedron inscribed in the same sphere (60.55%).[[11]](#cite_note-be-11) The resulting of both spheres' volumes initially began from the problem by ancient Greeks, determining which of two shapes has a larger volume: an icosahedron inscribed in a sphere, or a dodecahedron inscribed in the same sphere. Pet insurance data from Sweden puts the median lifespan of cats from the Persian group (Persians, Chinchilla, Himalayan and Exotic) at just above 12.5 years, while most cats live until they are about 15 years old. 76% of this group lived for 10 years or more and 52% lived for 12.5 years or more.[[68]](#cite_note-auto-68) A 2015 study looking at veterinary clinic data from England shows an average lifespan of 14.1.[[69]](#cite_note-69) A 2024 UK study found a life expectancy of 10.93 years for the Persian (9.63–12.23) compared to an overall of 11.74 years (11.61–11.87).[[70]](#cite_note-70)

Exaggerated illustration of Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun, marking that the orbital extreme points ([apoapsis](/wiki/Apoapsis "Apoapsis") and [periapsis](/wiki/Periapsis "Periapsis")) are not the same as the four seasonal extreme points, the [equinox](/wiki/Equinox "Equinox") and [solstice](/wiki/Solstice "Solstice")

Earth orbits the Sun at an average distance is about 150 million km (93 million mi). This makes Earth the third-closest planet to the Sun and part of the [inner Solar System](/wiki/Inner_Solar_System "Inner Solar System"). Its orbital distance is the basis for the [astronomical unit](/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") (AU) and is equal to roughly 8.3 [light minutes](/wiki/Light_minute "Light minute") or 380 times [Earth's distance to the Moon](/wiki/Lunar_distance "Lunar distance"). Earth orbits the Sun every 365.2564 mean [solar days](/wiki/Solar_day "Solar day"), or one [sidereal year](/wiki/Sidereal_year "Sidereal year"). With an apparent movement of the Sun in Earth's sky at a rate of about 1°/day eastward, which is one apparent Sun or Moon diameter every 12 hours. Due to this motion, on average it takes 24 hours—a solar day—for Earth to complete a full rotation about its axis so that the Sun returns to the [meridian](/wiki/Meridian_(astronomy) "Meridian (astronomy)"), slightly longer than the sidereal day.

The orbital speed of Earth averages at 29.7827 km/s (107,218 km/h; 66,622 mph), which is fast enough to travel a distance equal to Earth's diameter, about 12,742 km (7,918 mi), in seven minutes, and the distance from Earth to the Moon, 384,400 km (238,855 mi), in about 3.5 hours.[[3]](#cite_note-earth_fact_

Mechanism of 2011 Tōhoku earthquake

This megathrust earthquake was a recurrence of the mechanism of the earlier [869 Sanriku earthquake](/wiki/869_Sanriku_earthquake "869 Sanriku earthquake"), which has been estimated as having a magnitude of at least 8.4 Mw, which also created a large tsunami that inundated the Sendai plain.[[38]](#cite_note-w-39)[[74]](#cite_note-75)[[75]](#cite_note-76) Three tsunami deposits have been identified within the [Holocene](/wiki/Holocene "Holocene") sequence of the plain, all formed within the last 3,000 years, suggesting an 800 to 1,100 year recurrence interval for large tsunamigenic earthquakes. In 2001 it was reckoned that there was a high likelihood of a large tsunami hitting the Sendai plain as more than 1,100 years had then elapsed.[[76]](#cite_note-Minoura-77) In 2007, the probability of an earthquake with a magnitude of Mw 8.1–8.3 was estimated as 99% within the following 30 years.[[77]](#cite_note-Satake-78)

This earthquake occurred where the [Pacific plate](/wiki/Pacific_plate "Pacific plate") is [subducting](/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") under the plate beneath northern Honshu.[[66]](#cite_note-NYTimes-Chang2011-03-13-67)[[56]](#cite_note-grauniad-57) The Pacific plate, which moves at a rate of 8 to 9 cm (3.1 to 3.5 in) per year, dips under Honshu's underlying plate, building large amounts of [elastic energy](/wiki/Elastic_energy "Elastic energy"). This motion pushes the upper plate down until the accumulated stress causes a seismic slip-rupture event. The break caused the sea floor to rise by several meters.[[56]](#cite_note-grauniad-57) The magnitude of this earthquake was a surprise to some seismologists.[[78]](#cite_note-:2-79) A quake

Arata Isozaki :: Biography :: chunk_0001
Isozaki was born in Oita on the island of Kyushu and grew up in the era of [postwar Japan](/wiki/Postwar_Japan "Postwar Japan"),[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4) the eldest of four children of Toji and Tetsu Isozaki. His father was a prominent businessman.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) In 1945, he witnessed the destruction of [Hiroshima](/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima") on the shore opposite his hometown.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) When he accepted the [Pritzker Prize](/wiki/Pritzker_Architecture_Prize "Pritzker Architecture Prize") in 2019 he stated: "There was no architecture, no buildings, and not even a city. So my first experience of architecture was the void of architecture, and I began to consider how people might rebuild their homes and cities."[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2)

Isozaki completed his schooling at the [Oita Prefecture](/wiki/%C5%8Cita_(city) "Ōita (city)") Oita Uenogaoka High School (erstwhile Oita Junior High School). In 1954, he graduated from the [University of Tokyo](/wiki/University_of_Tokyo "University of Tokyo") majoring in Architecture and Engineering. He completed a doctoral program in architecture from the same university in 1961.[[1]](#cite_note-arata-1) Isozaki also worked under [Kenzo Tange](/wiki/Kenzo_Tange "Kenzo Tange") before establishing his firm in 1963.[[1]](#cite_note-arata-1)

Isozaki's early projects were influenced by European experiences with a style mixed between "New Brutalism" and "[Metabolist Architecture](/wiki/Metabolism_(architecture) "Metabolism (architecture)")" (Oita Medical Hall, 1959–1960), according to Reyner Banham. His style continued to evolve with buildings such as the Fujimi Country Club (1973–74) and Kitakyushu Central Library (1973–74). Later he developed a more modernistic style with buildings such as the [Art Tower of Mito](/wiki/Art_Tower_Mito "Art Tower Mito") (1986–90) and [Domus-Casa del Hombre](/wiki/Domus_(museum) "Domus (museum)") (1991–1995) in [Galicia, Spain](/wiki/Galicia,_Spain
